title: Building a first repertoire
blurb: Pick a small set of openings and learn them well: the London System as White, the Caro-Kann and …d5 as Black. Then learn the traps in them, and when to keep the tension.
deeperTitle: Common traps, and keeping the tension

core.title: A repertoire is a small plan
body: A **repertoire** is the few openings you always play. Learn the same ideas well instead of many lines badly.
Here is a first one: the **London System** as White, the **Caro-Kann** against 1.e4, and **…d5** against 1.d4. All three are solid, easy to learn, and light on theory.

core.prompt: How big should your first repertoire be?
options: One set-up as White, one answer to 1.e4 and one answer to 1.d4
Twenty openings, so you are ready for everything
Only the first move. Decide the rest in the game
core.explain: Three small choices cover every game. You will see the same positions again and again, and that is how you get good at them.

core.title: White: the London System
body: The London is a **set-up**, not a list of moves: pawns on d4, e3 and c3, a bishop on f4, knights on f3 and d2, and a bishop on d3. You can play it against almost anything.
The bishop goes out **before** the pawn move e3.

board.caption: The bishop on f4 stays outside the pawn chain and eyes c7.

core.prompt: White played e3 before bringing the bishop out. How many squares does the bishop on c1 attack now?
core.explain: Only b2, d2 and e3, all right behind its own pawns. The pawn on e3 locked the bishop in. That is why the London plays **Bf4** first.

core.prompt: Play the London set-up: d4, then Bf4, then e3, then Nf3. Black replies by itself.
core.hint: Centre pawn, bishop out, then the pawn that closes the diagonal, then the knight.
core.explain: That is the heart of the London. Next you add **c3**, **Nbd2** and **Bd3**, and castle. The same moves work against most Black set-ups.

core.prompt: Black’s bishop on d6 attacks your bishop on f4. Tap the square where your bishop should go.
core.explain: **Bg3** keeps the bishop, and if Black takes on g3 you recapture with the h-pawn. **Bxd6** trades it, which is fine too. Never leave the bishop on f4 to be taken for nothing.

core.prompt: Finish the London set-up: Nbd2, c3, Bd3, and castle. Black replies by itself.
core.hint: Knight to d2, pawn to c3, bishop to d3, then castle.
core.explain: Now every piece has a job: **c3** and **e3** hold the centre, the knights guard the middle, **Bd3** aims at the king, and the king is safe. You reach this against many Black set-ups.

core.prompt: You are Black. Play the Caro-Kann: c6, then d5, take on e4, and bring the bishop out to f5.
core.hint: Support the d5 push with a pawn move first.
core.explain: **…c6** prepares **…d5**. After the trade on e4, the bishop jumps out to **f5** before you play …e6.

core.prompt: In the Caro-Kann the d-pawn has left d7. How many squares does the bishop on c8 attack here?
core.explain: b7 (its own pawn), d7, e6, f5, g4 and h3. The diagonal is open, so the bishop can go outside the pawns. Compare the hemmed-in bishop on Day 8: it saw only 3.

core.prompt: Black has just taken on e4 and White recaptured. Tap the square where the c8 bishop belongs.
core.explain: **f5** is the classic square: the bishop looks at the whole diagonal, and it is outside the pawn chain, so …e6 will not shut it in.

core.prompt: White tries the Advance: 3.e5. Bring the bishop out before you close the pawn chain.
core.hint: Same idea as before: the c8 bishop goes outside the pawns.
core.explain: **Bf5** again. After 3.e5 the pawn chain is locked, so the bishop must be outside it **before** you play …e6. The idea is the same in every Caro-Kann.

core.prompt: You are Black against 1.d4. Play d5, Nf6, e6, and challenge White’s bishop with Bd6.
core.hint: Copy White’s centre first. Then knight, pawn, bishop.
core.explain: The same set-up works against the London and most other 1.d4 openings. **…Bd6** offers to trade White’s best bishop.

core.title: Your repertoire on one page
body: **White:** 1.d4, then Bf4, e3, Nf3, c3, Nbd2, Bd3 and castle.
**Black against 1.e4:** 1…c6, 2…d5, and bring the bishop out before …e6.
Write it down and keep it by your board.

core.title: Punish the mistake
core.intro: Both are mistakes you will see against your openings. Find the move that wins material.

puzzles.hint: After e3 your queen can see a long way. What is on h5?
puzzles.explain: **3.e3** opened the diagonal from d1 to h5. Black’s …Nh5 hoped to take your bishop, but it left the knight hanging: **Qxh5** wins it.

puzzles.hint: Which black piece lost its defender?
puzzles.explain: The bishop on d6 was defended only by the queen along the d-file. **…Nbd7** stepped in the way, so **Bxd6** wins a piece.

deeper.title: Traps are mistakes waiting to happen
body: A **trap** is a natural-looking move that loses. Most come from the same two mistakes: leaving a piece undefended, or missing a threat that looks harmless.
Know the traps in **your own** openings. They protect you, and sometimes they win you a game.

deeper.prompt: You are Black in the Caro-Kann. White’s queen has just gone to e2. White threatens a smothered checkmate. Find a move that stops it.
deeper.hint: The queen pins the pawn on e7, so a knight check on d6 cannot be taken. Give your king a square, or stop the knight.
deeper.explain: White threatens **Nd6#**: the pawn on e7 is pinned to the king, and the king is boxed in by its own pieces. **…e6**, **…Nb6**, **…Ndf6** and **…Qc7** all stop it. Most other moves, including the natural-looking **…Ngf6**, walk straight into it.

deeper.prompt: Black has just played Ngf6. Finish the game.
deeper.hint: A knight check that cannot be taken, because the pawn is pinned.
deeper.explain: **Nd6#**. The queen on e2 pins the e7 pawn, so it cannot take the knight, and Black’s own pieces cover every square the king could use.

deeper.title: Keeping the tension
body: Two pawns **attack each other** when each could take the other. That is **tension**. You do not have to capture. Often the side that captures first helps the other: a file opens, or the recapture is better.
Count first. If your pawn is defended enough, let your opponent decide.

board.caption: The pawns on c5 and d4 attack each other.

deeper.prompt: Black’s c5 attacks your d4 pawn. It is attacked once and defended twice. What is the best plan?
options: Keep the tension and play c3 to support d4
deeper.explain: The pawn is safe, so there is no need to take. **c3** adds a third defender and builds your set-up. Taking on c5 gives up your central pawn and lets Black recapture and develop at the same time.

deeper.title: Mistakes in your openings
deeper.intro: Early queen moves are the most common mistake. Take what is on offer.

puzzles.hint: Your bishop on f4 sees the black queen.
puzzles.explain: The London bishop attacks d6 along its diagonal. **Bxd6** wins the queen for a bishop.

puzzles.hint: A knight check that takes something.
puzzles.explain: The knight on e4 attacks d6. **Nxd6+** takes the queen with check.
Black brought the bishop out before taking on e4, and it is attacked by the e4 pawn. In the Caro-Kann the bishop goes to f5 **after** …dxe4.

deeper.title: Famous opening traps
deeper.intro: A king stuck in the middle is in danger. These are the traps that punish it. The second one is a classic.

puzzles.hint: The white king cannot move. Check from a knight cannot be blocked.
puzzles.explain: White's own pieces boxed the king in, and a knight's check cannot be blocked.

puzzles.hint: Black has just taken your queen. Start with a check.
puzzles.explain: This is **Légal's mate**. White gave up the queen so that Black's king would have to step into a net made of minor pieces.

deeper.prompt: You are Black. White threatens Qxf7 checkmate. Stop it.
deeper.hint: Defend f7, or chase the queen away.
deeper.explain: The simplest answers are **Qe7** or **Nh6**, which defend f7, or **g6**, which kicks the queen. Nf6 looks active, but it leaves f7 hanging.

deeper.prompt: Before every move in the opening, what should you ask?
options: Checks, captures and attacks, for me and for my opponent
deeper.explain: The checklist from Day 6 protects you from traps and finds them for you. Most traps are only a check, a capture or an attack that someone missed.
